# PV--BESS Dispatch Model: Verification and Validation Report

**Project:** PV-BESS Techno-Economic Analysis  
**Date:** June 2026  
**Stage:** v2 -- Real Data, Annual Rolling Horizon

---

## 1. Input Data Validation

The model relies on three real-world input datasets: (1) PVGIS-derived half-hourly PV
generation, (2) a synthetic household demand profile generated by the CREST Demand
Model, and (3) Octopus Agile half-hourly tariff prices. This section validates the PV
and demand inputs against independent external references. The Agile price data is taken
directly from Octopus Energy's published historical records and is not independently
validated here.

### 1.1 PV Generation

#### Data source

PV generation was obtained from the **PVGIS SARAH-3** satellite-derived radiation
database, provided by the European Commission Joint Research Centre. PVGIS SARAH-3 is
the reference dataset for solar resource assessment across Europe and is widely used in
peer-reviewed PV performance studies. The simulation was configured to match the
modelled system: 4 kWp, crystalline silicon, 35° tilt, south-facing (azimuth 0°), 14%
system losses, Glasgow (55.83°N, 4.28°W), year 2023.

#### Three-source annual comparison

The PVGIS annual specific yield was cross-checked against two independent measured
references:

1. **DESNZ Regional Renewable Statistics (2023):** UK Government data reporting annual
   electricity generation and installed capacity by local authority. For Glasgow City the
   figures are 17,604 MWh generated and 21.4 MWp installed capacity, giving a specific
   yield of **17,604 / 21.4 = 823 kWh/kWp**. This dataset is derived from Feed-in
   Tariff (FiT) and Export Guarantee generation meter readings -- actual metered output
   from real installations.

2. **Sheffield Solar PV_Live (PES 18, SP Distribution, 2023):** PV_Live uses machine
   learning to estimate half-hourly PV generation from a sample of metered GB
   installations. PES region 18 covers SP Distribution -- south Scotland including
   Glasgow. The full-year 2023 half-hourly timeseries was retrieved via the
   `pvlive-api` Python library and normalised by the installed capacity field
   (`installedcapacity_mwp`) to compute a specific yield of **757 kWh/kWp**.

| Source | Annual specific yield (kWh/kWp) | Type |
|---|---|---|
| PVGIS SARAH-3 (simulated) | **847** | Satellite-derived simulation |
| DESNZ Regional Stats, Glasgow City (2023) | **823** | Metered FiT/SEG data |
| PV_Live, PES 18 SP Distribution (2023) | **757** | ML-estimated regional outturn |

The PVGIS estimate of 847 kWh/kWp agrees with the DESNZ metered figure to within
**+2.9%**. The wider gap against PV_Live (+11.9%) is expected and explained by
geographic scope: PES 18 covers all of south Scotland -- a much larger and more
climatically diverse region than Glasgow City -- including older, degraded, and
variably-oriented installations that pull the normalised yield below the idealised
single-system PVGIS simulation. The PVGIS input therefore represents a plausible
upper bound on PV output for a well-maintained new 4 kWp installation.

The systematic winter divergence (November--December: ~40--45% above PV_Live) arises
because real-world PV yield at low sun angles is disproportionately reduced by soiling,
shading from surrounding structures, and increased spectral mismatch relative to the
clean PVGIS simulation. This means the model's winter dispatch behaviour is modestly
optimistic: the real battery would have less PV available to self-consume or store
during winter months, and the Agile price-arbitrage role of the battery in winter is
correspondingly larger in practice than the simulation predicts.

#### Monthly comparison

![Monthly PV specific yield: PVGIS SARAH-3 vs PV_Live measured outturn](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 1.** Monthly specific yield (kWh/kWp) for 2023: PVGIS SARAH-3 simulated
output for a 4 kWp south-facing Glasgow system (orange) vs Sheffield Solar PV_Live
measured outturn for SP Distribution PES region 18 (blue). The DESNZ Glasgow City
annual total is annotated in the figure. Agreement is closest in summer (June--July:
~2--3% difference) and widest in winter (November--December: ~40--45% difference).

### 1.2 Household Demand

#### Data source

Household demand was generated using the **CREST Demand Model v2.3.3**, developed by
Loughborough University (Richardson, Thomson & Infield, 2010; Thomson & Infield, 2007).
CREST is a stochastic bottom-up model that simulates one-minute electricity demand for a
single UK dwelling by modelling occupancy transitions and the stochastic activation of
individual appliances. It has been extensively validated against measured UK household
data in the published literature and is a widely used reference tool for UK domestic
energy demand research.

The model was configured as follows:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Number of residents | 3 |
| Primary heating system | Gas central heating (index 1) |
| Appliance ownership year | 2023 |
| Calendar year | 2023 |

The calendar year was set to 2023 -- matching the PV generation and Agile price data --
so that the weekday/weekend flag assigned to each simulated day is correctly aligned with
the 2023 Agile price structure. An earlier draft used a 2025 calendar year, which
introduced a systematic weekday/weekend misalignment (1 January 2025 is a Wednesday; 1
January 2023 is a Sunday) affecting the correlation between high-demand and high-price
periods. This has been corrected in the current dataset by regenerating the profile
under the 2023 calendar.

The 1-minute output from the CREST `Results - aggregated` sheet was averaged into 48
half-hourly values per day and assembled into an annual CSV using the
`generate_demand_profile.py` automation script.

#### Annual total comparison

The generated profile has an annual total of **4,837 kWh/yr**. For context:

| Benchmark | kWh/yr | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Ofgem TDCV -- Low | 1,800 | All household sizes |
| Ofgem TDCV -- Medium | 2,900 | All household sizes |
| Ofgem TDCV -- High | 4,300 | All household sizes |
| **CREST profile** | **4,837** | 3-person, gas-heated household |
| BEIS national mean (ECUK, 2023) | ~3,500 | Average across all domestic meters |

The CREST consumption sits modestly above the Ofgem "high" band. This is consistent
with the household configuration: a 3-occupant dwelling is above the national average
household size (~2.4 persons), and the appliance set -- which includes a tumble dryer
and dishwasher -- adds approximately 700--1,000 kWh/yr relative to a comparable
household without these appliances. The BEIS national mean of ~3,500 kWh/yr is averaged
across all domestic meters including single-occupant flats and is therefore an
unsuitable direct comparator for a 3-person household. The CREST profile represents an
above-average but realistic domestic electricity consumer consistent with the configured
household archetype.

The gas central heating configuration (heating index 1) means there is no electric space
heating in the profile. This is appropriate for the majority of UK domestic PV--BESS
installations, which are typically retrofitted into gas-heated homes. It also explains
the relatively flat seasonal demand variation observed below: electricity use is
dominated by appliances and lighting rather than space heating.

## 2. Model Verification Tests

The dispatch model is verified through a suite of 17 automated unit tests in two files:
`tests/test_data_loader.py` (7 tests covering data ingestion and alignment) and
`tests/test_model.py` (10 tests covering the MILP formulation). All 17 tests pass.

### 2.1 Data loader tests

These tests verify that the three data sources load correctly onto the canonical
half-hourly index with correct units, no missing values, and sensible ranges.

| Test | Assertion |
|---|---|
| `test_canonical_index_length_non_leap` | 2023 index has exactly 17,520 periods at 30-min frequency |
| `test_canonical_index_length_leap` | 2024 index has exactly 17,568 periods |
| `test_load_pv_aligned_and_in_kw` | PV series: correct length, no nulls, non-negative, max <= 4.5 kW, zero at night |
| `test_load_pv_halfhours_repeat_hourly` | Each hourly PVGIS value fills both its half-hours identically (forward-fill) |
| `test_load_demand_aligned_and_positive` | Demand: correct length, no nulls, non-negative, indexed on 2023 canonical index |
| `test_load_agile_prices_converted_and_complete` | Prices in GBP/kWh, no nulls, import can be negative, export non-negative |
| `test_load_all_combines_columns` | Combined DataFrame: correct columns, correct length, no nulls anywhere |

### 2.2 Original model tests (inherited from Stage 1)

Five tests were written during Stage 1 to verify physical correctness of the MILP
formulation on synthetic data. These continue to pass throughout Stage 2.

| Test | Scenario | Assertion |
|---|---|---|
| `test_flat_price_no_pv_no_cycling` | Flat prices, no PV, no degradation cost | Battery does not cycle; all demand met by grid import |
| `test_price_arbitrage_charges_cheap_discharges_peak` | Two-tier prices, no PV, zero export price | Charge concentrated in cheap hours; discharge in peak hours |
| `test_soc_within_bounds` | Synthetic data, degradation cost 0.01 GBP/kWh | SOC never violates [soc_min, soc_max] at any timestep (tolerance 1e-4) |
| `test_energy_balance_satisfied` | Synthetic data, degradation cost 0.05 GBP/kWh | PV + import + discharge = demand + export + charge at every timestep (within 0.1 W) |
| `test_no_simultaneous_charge_discharge` | Synthetic data, degradation cost 0.05 GBP/kWh | Product of p_charge x p_discharge < 1e-4 at every timestep |

### 2.3 New model tests

Five additional tests were added to verify specific physical behaviours and quantitative
correctness not covered by the original suite.

#### Test 1 -- SOC dynamics: quantitative increment verification

**Purpose.** The original `test_soc_within_bounds` checked only that the SOC stayed
within the allowed range. This test verifies the *magnitude* of the SOC increment from
a known charging event against the value computed analytically from the governing
difference equation -- confirming that the constraint coefficients are correctly
specified.

**Scenario.** Two half-hourly timesteps (dt = 0.5 h). PV = 3 kW, demand = 0 kW, and the
grid connection is disabled (`max_grid_kw = 0`). With no export possible and no demand
to serve, the energy balance constraint uniquely determines p_charge = 3 kW at both
timesteps. Battery: capacity = 10 kWh, eta_c = 0.95, soc_init = 0.0.

**Analytical expected value:**

    delta_SOC = (eta_c * p_charge * dt) / capacity
              = (0.95 * 3.0 * 0.5) / 10.0
              = 0.1425 per timestep

**Assertions.** `soc_end[0] = 0.1425` and `soc_end[1] = 0.2850`, both within 1e-5.

---

#### Test 2 -- Import/export mutual exclusivity under negative import price

**Purpose.** The binary variable `grid_import_on[t]` prevents simultaneous grid import
and export. Negative Agile import prices (periods when the system operator pays consumers
to absorb surplus wind generation) create the strongest incentive for an LP without the
binary to exploit both simultaneously for unlimited profit. This test confirms the binary
constraint is enforced under exactly this condition.

**Scenario.** Four half-hourly timesteps with mixed import prices including two negative
values: `import_price = [-0.10, 0.10, -0.05, 0.08]` GBP/kWh; `export_price = 0.05`
GBP/kWh throughout; degradation cost = 0.05 GBP/kWh.

**Assertion.** For every timestep t: NOT (p_import[t] > 1e-4 AND p_export[t] > 1e-4).

---

#### Test 3 -- Terminal SOC exact equality

**Purpose.** In single-day mode (`terminal_soc_equals_initial = True`), the battery
must end the day at exactly its initial SOC to make the accounting self-contained. The
original tests did not check this equality explicitly.

**Scenario.** Standard 24-hour synthetic dataset, degradation cost 0.05 GBP/kWh.

**Assertion.** `|soc_end[-1] - soc_init| < 1e-5`.

---

#### Test 4 -- Zero power flows when PV exactly meets demand

**Purpose.** When PV generation equals demand at every half-hour, the household is
self-sufficient and there is no economic incentive to import, export, or cycle the
battery. A positive degradation cost ensures the optimiser does not cycle gratuitously.

**Scenario.** 48 half-hourly timesteps; PV = demand = 0.5 kW throughout; degradation
cost = 0.05 GBP/kWh.

**Assertion.** Sum of all power flows
(p_charge + p_discharge + p_import + p_export) < 1e-4 kW.

---

#### Test 5 -- Optimal cost matches analytical solution

**Purpose.** Verifies that the solver finds the *provably optimal* dispatch, not merely
a feasible solution. A two-timestep scenario is constructed for which the minimum cost
is uniquely determined analytically, and the solver result is compared against it.

**Scenario.** Two half-hourly timesteps (dt = 0.5 h).

- Period 0 (cheap): demand = 0 kW, PV = 0 kW, import_price = 0.07 GBP/kWh, export_price = 0.
- Period 1 (peak): demand = 1 kW, PV = 0 kW, import_price = 0.28 GBP/kWh, export_price = 0.

Battery: eta_c = eta_d = 0.95, soc_init = 0.0, soc_min = 0.0, soc_max = 1.0,
degradation_cost = 0, no terminal SOC constraint.

**Analytical derivation.** The optimal strategy is to pre-charge in period 0 and
discharge to serve the full peak demand in period 1 with zero grid import in period 1.
The required charge power accounts for round-trip losses:

    p_charge[0] = demand / (eta_c * eta_d) = 1.0 / 0.9025 ≈ 1.108 kW

    import_cost = import_price[0] * p_charge[0] * dt
                = 0.07 * (1/0.9025) * 0.5
                ≈ GBP 0.03878

**Assertions.** `p_import[1] < 1e-4` (peak demand served entirely from battery) and
`|import_cost - 0.03878| < 1e-4`.

**Note on cross-solver validation.** A direct comparison of results between two
independent MILP solvers was intended but was not possible in the current environment:
only one MILP-capable solver is available (`scipy.optimize.milp`). Test 5 above serves
the same validation purpose -- it confirms the solver finds the analytically verified
global optimum rather than a suboptimal feasible solution.

## 3. Mathematical Formulation Justification

### 3.1 Modelling framework

The optimisation problem is implemented in **CVXPY** (Diamond & Boyd, 2016), an
open-source Python-embedded algebraic modelling language for convex optimisation. CVXPY
allows the problem to be expressed in natural mathematical form and automatically
translates it into the standard solver input format. It is solver-agnostic: the same
model definition can be passed to any compatible solver without modification.

CVXPY is a peer-reviewed, actively maintained library used extensively in academic
energy systems research. Its constraint verification layer catches modelling errors (such
as non-convex or incorrectly typed constraints) at problem construction time, before the
solver is called, providing an additional layer of correctness assurance.

The solver used is **`scipy.optimize.milp`** (SciPy >= 1.7), which implements
branch-and-bound for mixed-integer linear programmes. For problems of the size used here
(48 binary variables, ~300 continuous variables per day) solve times are of order
10--50 ms.

> **Reference:** Diamond, S. & Boyd, S. (2016). CVXPY: A Python-Embedded Modeling
> Language for Convex Optimization. *Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 17(83), 1--5.

---

### 3.2 Decision variables

At each half-hourly timestep t in {0, ..., T-1} the optimiser controls six variables:

| Variable | Units | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `p_charge[t]` | kW | Battery charging power |
| `p_discharge[t]` | kW | Battery discharging power |
| `p_import[t]` | kW | Grid import power |
| `p_export[t]` | kW | Grid export power |
| `soc[t]` | fraction of capacity | State of charge at start of period t |
| `grid_import_on[t]` | binary {0,1} | 1 if importing from grid; 0 if exporting |

---

### 3.3 Constraints and their physical meaning

**Initial SOC**

    soc[0] = soc_init

Sets the battery state of charge at the start of the simulation to the known initial
value (default 50%). This is a boundary condition that makes the optimisation problem
well-posed.

---

**Terminal SOC (single-day mode)**

    soc[T] = soc_init    (when terminal_soc_equals_initial = True)

Forces the battery to end the simulated period at the same SOC it started. This makes
each day a self-contained accounting unit and prevents the optimiser from treating the
initial stored energy as a free resource that flatters savings. In the annual rolling
horizon this constraint is disabled; the end-of-day SOC is carried forward as the
initial SOC of the following day.

---

**SOC dynamics -- discrete-time Coulomb counting**

    soc[t+1] = soc[t] + (eta_c * p_charge[t] - p_discharge[t] / eta_d) * dt / capacity

This is the standard **discrete-time Coulomb counting model** (Plett, 2015): the SOC
changes in proportion to the net charge flux through the battery terminals, corrected
for charging efficiency eta_c (losses occur on the way in) and discharging efficiency
eta_d (losses occur on the way out). It is a linear difference equation that is directly
embeddable in a linear programme without approximation.

The round-trip efficiency is eta_c * eta_d = 0.95 * 0.95 = 0.9025, so 9.75% of energy
is lost per full cycle.

> **Reference:** Plett, G.L. (2015). *Battery Management Systems, Volume 1: Battery
> Modeling*. Artech House, Chapter 3.

---

**SOC bounds**

    soc_min <= soc[t] <= soc_max    for all t

Enforces the usable state-of-charge window (default 10%--90% of nominal capacity).
Operating below soc_min accelerates deep-discharge degradation; operating above soc_max
accelerates overcharge degradation. These bounds match the protection settings of real
battery management systems.

---

**Power limits**

    0 <= p_charge[t] <= P_max_charge
    0 <= p_discharge[t] <= P_max_discharge    for all t

Enforces the inverter power rating (3 kW each direction). This matches the physical
maximum charge/discharge rate of the modelled system and prevents the optimiser from
suggesting impossible power flows.

---

**Energy balance**

    PV[t] + p_import[t] + p_discharge[t] = demand[t] + p_export[t] + p_charge[t]
    for all t

Conservation of energy at the household node at every timestep: every kilowatt arriving
(from PV generation, the grid, or the battery) must be accounted for on the right-hand
side (demand served, exported to the grid, or stored in the battery). This is the
central physical constraint from which all dispatch decisions flow.

---

**Import/export mutual exclusivity -- the MILP constraint**

    p_import[t] <= M * u[t]
    p_export[t] <= M * (1 - u[t])    for all t

where M = 20 kW is the grid connection capacity (big-M parameter) and u[t] in {0,1} is
the binary variable. A domestic electricity meter cannot simultaneously import and export
power. The binary variable u[t] enforces this: when u[t] = 1 import is unrestricted
but export is forced to zero; when u[t] = 0 the reverse applies.

This constraint is the reason the problem is a **Mixed-Integer Linear Programme (MILP)**
rather than a pure LP. It is physically necessary: without it the model is unbounded
whenever export price exceeds import price, because the LP solver would import and export
unlimited power simultaneously for unlimited profit. This scenario occurs routinely in
the Agile tariff dataset, where import prices are frequently negative. The binary is
therefore not a modelling choice but a physical requirement.

Note that simultaneous charge and discharge does *not* require a separate binary
variable. Round-trip losses mean it is always suboptimal to cycle energy through the
battery needlessly when a positive degradation cost is present, so the LP naturally
avoids it for non-degenerate inputs.

---

### 3.4 Objective function and throughput degradation model

    min  sum_t  dt * [ lambda_buy[t] * p_import[t]
                      - lambda_sell[t] * p_export[t]
                      + c_deg * (p_charge[t] + p_discharge[t]) ]

The three terms represent:

- **Import cost:** payment to the grid for each kWh consumed at the prevailing
  time-of-use Agile price.
- **Export revenue** (subtracted): income from surplus energy sent to the grid at the
  Agile export price.
- **Throughput degradation penalty:** a monetary cost assigned to every kWh passing
  through the battery in either direction, representing the amortised battery replacement
  cost spread across total warranted lifetime throughput.

The **linear throughput degradation model** was selected because it is directly
embeddable in the LP objective without approximation. Rainflow cycle counting -- a more
physically accurate degradation model -- is non-convex and cannot be incorporated into a
linear programme; it can only be applied post-hoc to the solved SOC trajectory as a
validation step.

The default value c_deg = 0.05 GBP/kWh (5 p/kWh) is consistent with a battery having
a replacement cost of approximately GBP 2,000 and a warranted lifetime throughput of
40,000 kWh, representative of current domestic lithium-ion systems.

The degradation term plays a central role in the research question: it forces the
optimiser to evaluate whether the arbitrage margin from a given dispatch cycle exceeds
the wear cost. It also naturally suppresses simultaneous charge and discharge, since the
round-trip cost plus degradation penalty always exceeds zero net benefit for
self-cycling.

> **Reference:** Xu, B., Oudalov, A., Ulbig, A., Andersson, G. & Kirschen, D.S. (2018).
> Factoring the Cycle Aging Cost of Batteries Participating in Electricity Markets.
> *IEEE Transactions on Power Systems*, 33(2), 2248--2259.
